summary: This informational document gives example call flows showing how Session Initiation Protocol uses TLS and S/MIME. It helps implementers build interoperable software and includes certificates used in the examples so tests can be repeated. The examples show messages step by step.

eli5.summary: This is a worked example book for secure phone calls over the internet, showing every message in order. Programmers can copy the steps to check their own work.

subtitle: Worked examples showing how SIP uses TLS and S/MIME to protect messages.

tldr.problem: Developers building SIP software that uses TLS and S/MIME encryption need test vectors and example messages to verify their implementations work correctly with other systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6216 provides detailed example call flows showing every step of TLS connections and S/MIME signed or encrypted messages, along with test certificates that implementers can use for interoperability testing.
tldr.outcome: This informational document helps implementers build interoperable secure SIP software and includes certificates and scripts for setting up test environments.

today: RFC 6216 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains a reference for implementing SIP security. However, modern deployments should note that SHA-1 signatures are now considered weak; implementations should prefer SHA-256 or stronger hash algorithms.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6216 is a practical guide for software developers building SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) implementations that use TLS (Transport Layer Security) and S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions). SIP is a signaling protocol for establishing voice and video calls.

The RFC provides detailed example call flows and message dumps that show exactly how TLS handshakes work in SIP and how to sign, encrypt, or both sign and encrypt message bodies using S/MIME. It also includes test certificates and scripts for creating more certificates, so implementers can test their code against known good examples at interoperability events.
sections.eli5: This guide shows exactly what messages go back and forth when two programs set up a secure phone call and how they prove they are who they say they are.

sections.title: Certificates and Trust
sections.content:
Before TLS or S/MIME can protect SIP messages, both parties need certificates that prove their identity. The RFC shows three types: CA (certification authority) certificates that sign others, host certificates used in TLS connections, and user certificates used to sign or encrypt message bodies.

A CA certificate is self-signed and marked with the Basic Constraints extension as a CA, so it can sign other certificates. The CA used in the examples is named 'Sipit Test Certificate Authority' and uses a 2048-bit RSA public key. Host certificates (for example, one for example.com) include a Subject Alternative Name with the hostname or SIP URI, and are signed by the Sipit CA. User certificates (for example, one for fluffy@example.com) also include a Subject Alternative Name listing the user's URIs (sip:, im:, pres: addresses) so they work with instant messaging systems.
sections.eli5: A certificate is like a passport: it shows who you are and who signed it to prove you are telling the truth. The RFC shows example passports for hosts and users that all trust the same certification authority.

sections.title: TLS Connection and MESSAGE Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC shows a detailed TLS handshake between two SIP servers. The client sends a ClientHello proposing several cipher suites (ways to encrypt), the server picks one and sends back its certificate, and then they exchange keys. The example uses TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA. Once the TLS connection is set up, a SIP MESSAGE request (instant message) can be sent over it. The MESSAGE request uses a SIPS URI (the 's' means TLS is required) and the Via header indicates that TLS was used.

The server's certificate includes not only the hostname (example.net) in the Subject Alternative Name but also a SIP URI to identify its role in SIP communications. The text notes that clients should reuse TLS connections for multiple messages rather than opening a new TLS connection for every message, citing RFC 5923 on connection reuse.
sections.eli5: Two servers shake hands using TLS, agree on a secret way to scramble messages, and then send and receive instant messages encrypted with that secret.

sections.title: S/MIME Message Bodies
sections.content:
S/MIME allows the body of a SIP message to be signed, encrypted, or both. In a signed message, the Content-Type is multipart/signed with a boundary separating the plain-text message body from a signature part. The signature is computed over the MIME headers and message body, but not over the boundary lines.

The RFC shows an example MESSAGE request containing 'Hello!' as a signed body. The signature uses SHA-1 and RSA encryption. It notes that two encodings are valid: one with the SHA-1 parameters set to NULL (historical), and the preferred form omitting the NULL (per RFC 3370). In encrypted messages, the Content-Type is application/pkcs7-mime with smime-type=enveloped-data, and the body is encrypted using AES128-CBC. Combined signed-and-encrypted messages wrap the encrypted content in a multipart/signed container to sign the encryption.
sections.eli5: Messages can be sealed with a digital signature (proving who sent it), locked with a key (so only the right person can read it), or both.

sections.title: Observed Issues and Testing
sections.content:
The RFC documents problems found at SIPit (SIP Interoperability Testing) events. Some clients incorrectly implement only SSLv3 instead of TLS. Many clients accept expired certificates without warning. Certificate path validation (checking that the authority chain is trusted) is complex and easy to get wrong; the RFC warns that implementations must carefully follow RFC 5280.

When matching certificates to identities, clients must check the Subject Alternative Name: for TLS, the hostname must match a dNSName in subjectAltName (exact match, no wildcards), or if there are no dNSNames, the most specific CommonName in the Subject field (exact or wildcard). For S/MIME, the peer's SIP URI must appear as a uniformResourceIdentifier in the Subject Alternative Name. The RFC lists 17 test scenarios covering good and bad certificates to verify correct behavior.
sections.eli5: Programmers often make mistakes checking whether a certificate really belongs to the right person. These test cases help find those mistakes.
